## Discussion

In this study we evaluated the genetic contribution of the MC system to FA assessed with the YFAS 2.0 via MC4R polymorphisms in a clinical population. The comparison of the groups confirmed data previously reported in the literature. In our sample, a significantly higher percentage of female patients and a diagnosis of BED were evident in the group with FA than in the group without FA. This result is in line with community studies that directly compared individuals with obesity and FA with individuals with obesity but without FA [[76](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR76 "Davis C. The epidemiology and genetics of binge eating disorder (BED). CNS Spectr. 2015;20:522–9.")]. As noted, BED and FA often overlap and are common in individuals with high body weight [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR9 "Carbone EA, Aloi M, Rania M, de Filippis R, Quirino D, Fiorentino TV et al. The relationship of food addiction with binge eating disorder and obesity: A network analysis study. Appetite. 2023;190."), [77](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR77 "Ivezaj V, White MA, Grilo CM. Examining binge-eating disorder and food addiction in adults with overweight and obesity. Obes (Silver Spring). 2016;24:2064–9.")]. Patients with FA, particularly those with high-functioning addiction and fully addiction profile, exhibited more anxiety, depressive symptoms, altered eating behaviors and emotion dysregulation [[78](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR78 "Aloi M, Liuzza MT, Rania M, Carbone EA, de Filippis R, Gearhardt AN et al. Using latent class analysis to identify different clinical profiles according to food addiction symptoms in obesity with and without binge eating disorder. J Behav Addict 2024;13.")]. Numerous studies found that people who meet the criteria for both BED and FA are likely to report more frequent bingeing episodes, depressive symptoms, intense food cravings more than those with BED alone [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR11 "Granero R, Hilker I, Agüera Z, Jiménez-Murcia S, Sauchelli S, Islam MA, et al. Food addiction in a Spanish sample of eating disorders: DSM-5 diagnostic subtype differentiation and validation data. Eur Eat Disord Rev. 2014;22:389–96."), [76](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR76 "Davis C. The epidemiology and genetics of binge eating disorder (BED). CNS Spectr. 2015;20:522–9.")] suggesting that this comorbidity may represent a different phenotype of BED, characterized by not only a greater and more severe psychopathology [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR14 "Gearhardt AN, White MA, Masheb RM, Morgan PT, Crosby RD, Grilo CM. An examination of the food addiction construct in obese patients with binge eating disorder. Int J Eat Disord. 2012;45:657–63."), [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR15 "Sommer LM, Halbeisen G, Erim Y, Paslakis G. Two of a kind?? Mapping the psychopathological space between obesity with and without binge eating disorder. Nutrients 2021;13."), [18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR18 "Gearhardt AN, White MA, Masheb RM, Grilo CM. An examination of food addiction in a Racially diverse sample of obese patients with binge eating disorder in primary care settings. Compr Psychiatry. 2013;54:500–5."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR26 "Burrows T, Skinner J, McKenna R, Rollo M, Food, Addiction. Binge Eating Disorder, and Obesity: Is There a Relationship? Behavioral sciences (Basel, Switzerland) 2017;7.")] but also serious health consequences such as impaired metabolic response [[79](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR79 "Rania M, Caroleo M, Carbone EA, Ricchio M, Pelle MC, Zaffina I et al. Reactive hypoglycemia in binge eating disorder, food addiction, and the comorbid phenotype: unravelling the metabolic drive to disordered eating behaviours. J Eat Disord 2023;11.")]. Recently, a study involving 502 individuals found that 8.5% met the criteria for BED, 16.6% met the criteria for FA, 10.1% met the criteria for both BED + FA, and 64.8% met neither (controls) [[77](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR77 "Ivezaj V, White MA, Grilo CM. Examining binge-eating disorder and food addiction in adults with overweight and obesity. Obes (Silver Spring). 2016;24:2064–9.")]. All the three groups (FA, BED and FA + BED) scored significantly higher on eating disorder psychopathology, impulsivity, self-control than controls, while patients with FA and FA + BED groups reported significantly higher depression scores than the control group. Emotion dysregulation and deficits in interoceptive awareness can also contribute to FA leading people with FA to consume certain foods in an attempt to regulate their emotions [[80](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR80 "Li Cshan, Sinha R. Inhibitory control and emotional stress regulation: neuroimaging evidence for frontal-limbic dysfunction in psycho-stimulant addiction. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2008;32:581–97.")]. In our sample, BED diagnosis had a significant effect on depression in FA group. It was demonstrated that the desire for certain food can also be elicited by negative emotional states and food can be used to regulate negative mood [[80](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR80 "Li Cshan, Sinha R. Inhibitory control and emotional stress regulation: neuroimaging evidence for frontal-limbic dysfunction in psycho-stimulant addiction. Neurosci Biobehav Rev. 2008;32:581–97.")]. On the other hand, negative emotions can promote a craving for highly palatable foods preceding binge eating episodes [[81](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR81 "Meule A, Lutz A, Vögele C, Kübler A. Women with elevated food addiction symptoms show accelerated reactions, but no impaired inhibitory control, in response to pictures of high-calorie food-cues. Eat Behav. 2012;13:423–8."), [82](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR82 "Berg KC, Peterson CB, Crosby RD, Cao L, Crow SJ, Engel SG, et al. Relationship between daily affect and overeating-only, loss of control eating-only, and binge eating episodes in obese adults. Psychiatry Res. 2014;215:185–91.")].

Although previous studies have examined the link between MC4R variants and eating-related behaviors or obesity-related phenotypes [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR44 "Yilmaz Z, Davis C, Loxton NJ, Kaplan AS, Levitan RD, Carter JC, et al. Association between MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism and overeating behaviors. Int J Obes (Lond). 2015;39:114–20."), [83](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR83 "Obregón AM, Oyarce K, Santos JL, Valladares M, Goldfield G. Association of the melanocortin 4 receptor gene rs17782313 polymorphism with rewarding value of food and eating behavior in Chilean children. J Physiol Biochem. 2017;73:29–35."),[84](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR84 "Chermon D, Birk R. Predisposition of the common MC4R rs17782313 female carriers to elevated obesity and interaction with eating habits. Genes (Basel) 2023;14."),[85](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR85 "Alvarez-Martin C, Caballero FF, de la Iglesia R, Alonso-Aperte E. Association of MC4R rs17782313 genotype with energy intake and appetite: A systematic review and Meta-analysis. Nutr Rev. 2025;83:e931–46."),[86](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR86 "Rahati S, Qorbani M, Naghavi A, Pishva H. Association and interaction of the MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism with plasma ghrelin, GLP-1, cortisol, food intake and eating behaviors in overweight/obese Iranian adults. BMC Endocr Disord 2022;22.")], the most important and innovative finding of this study is the association between the MC4R polymorphisms, and the presence of FA as assessed with the YFAS 2.0 in our sample that, to the best of our knowledge, no previous studies have investigated.

In this study we evaluated the genetic contribution of the MC system to FA assessed with the YFAS 2.0 via MC4R polymorphisms in a clinical population.

In our sample the genotype and the allelic frequencies are superimposable to that of general population for all the MC4R variants allowing us to generalize our results. The rs17782313 of the MC4R showed an association with the FA and the CC genotype was more prevalent in patients with FA than the group without FA.

The rs17782313 is one of the SNPs of the MC4R gene most studied. This SNP has two alleles, T and C, where the T allele is the ancestral one and the C allele is the risk allele. The rs17782313 has been linked with increased BMI, increased waist circumference [[87](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR87 "Loos RJF. The genetic epidemiology of melanocortin 4 receptor variants. Eur J Pharmacol. 2011;660:156–64.")], insulin resistance [[88](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR88 "Tschritter O, Haupt A, Preissl H, Ketterer C, Hennige AM, Sartorius T et al. An Obesity Risk SNP (rs17782313) near the MC4R Gene Is Associated with Cerebrocortical Insulin Resistance in Humans. J Obes. 2011;2011.")], diabetes mellitus type 2 and lipid intake [[89](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR89 "Khalilitehrani A, Qorbani M, Hosseini S, Pishva H. The association of MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism with dietary intake in Iranian adults. Gene. 2015;563:125–9.")]. In particular, the C allele has already been demonstrated to give a higher risk for weight gain than the T allele [[90](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR90 "Cauchi S, Stutzmann F, Cavalcanti-Proença C, Durand E, Pouta A, Hartikainen AL, et al. Combined effects of MC4R and FTO common genetic variants on obesity in European general populations. J Mol Med. 2009;87:537–46."), [91](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR91 "Bordoni L, Marchegiani F, Piangerelli M, Napolioni V, Gabbianelli R. Obesity-related genetic polymorphisms and adiposity indices in a young Italian population. IUBMB Life. 2017;69:98–105.")] and it was related to food intake, overeating, severe binge eating [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR44 "Yilmaz Z, Davis C, Loxton NJ, Kaplan AS, Levitan RD, Carter JC, et al. Association between MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism and overeating behaviors. Int J Obes (Lond). 2015;39:114–20."), [48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR48 "Magno FCCM, Guaraná HC, da Fonseca ACP, Pedrosa AP, Zembrzuski VM, Cabello PH et al. Eat Weight Disorders. 2020.")], pinches or snacking [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR52 "Stutzmann F, Cauchi S, Durand E, Calvacanti-Proença C, Pigeyre M, Hartikainen AL, et al. Common genetic variation near MC4R is associated with eating behaviour patterns in European populations. Int J Obes. 2009;33:373–8.")], emotional eating [[86](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR86 "Rahati S, Qorbani M, Naghavi A, Pishva H. Association and interaction of the MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism with plasma ghrelin, GLP-1, cortisol, food intake and eating behaviors in overweight/obese Iranian adults. BMC Endocr Disord 2022;22.")], lower satiety responsiveness and higher uncontrolled eating scores compared to non-carriers [[83](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR83 "Obregón AM, Oyarce K, Santos JL, Valladares M, Goldfield G. Association of the melanocortin 4 receptor gene rs17782313 polymorphism with rewarding value of food and eating behavior in Chilean children. J Physiol Biochem. 2017;73:29–35.")]. Few studies have reported an association between rs17782313 C allele and other eating behaviors (i.e., grazing, hyperphagia) with mixed and unclear results [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR53 "Valette M, Bellisle F, Carette C, Poitou C, Dubern B, Paradis G, et al. Eating behaviour in obese patients with melanocortin-4 receptor mutations: A literature review. Int J Obes. 2013;Int J Obes Lond:1027–35.")]. It was observed that the MC4R play a role in energy intake and dietary high-fat/high-sucrose preference [[92](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR92 "Mul JD, Van Boxtel R, Bergen DJM, Brans MAD, Brakkee JH, Toonen PW, et al. Melanocortin receptor 4 deficiency affects body weight regulation, grooming behavior, and substrate preference in the rat. Obes (Silver Spring). 2012;20:612–21.")] and that rs17782313 variant is associated with higher energy intake, especially higher percentage of fat energy [[93](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR93 "Samama P, Rumennik L, Grippo JF. The melanocortin receptor MCR4 controls fat consumption. Regul Pept. 2003;113:85–8.")]. The MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism has been shown to decrease proopiomelanocortin (POMC) expression and to be related with morbid obesity, since POMC can influence regulatory mechanisms that stimulate satiety [[94](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR94 "Srivastava A, Mittal B, Prakash J, Narain VS, Natu SM, Srivastava N. Evaluation of MC4R [rs17782313, rs17700633], AGRP [rs3412352] and POMC [rs1042571] polymorphisms with obesity in Northern India. Oman Med J. 2014;29:114–8.")]. A possible explanation of this association may be due to the MC4R involvement in the homeostatic and non-homeostatic mechanisms of food intake. Indeed, the MC4R is co-expressed with dopamine receptors in hypothalamic area [[95](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR95 "Yoon YR, Baik JH. Melanocortin 4 receptor and dopamine D2 receptor expression in brain areas involved in food intake. Endocrinol Metab (Seoul). 2015;30:576–83.")] and is highly expressed in the mesolimbic system [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR38 "Kishi T, Aschkenasi CJ, Lee CE, Mountjoy KG, Saper CB, Elmquist JK. Expression of melanocortin 4 receptor mRNA in the central nervous system of the rat. J Comp Neurol. 2003;457:213–35.")] where can modulate dopamine release [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR30 "Lindblom J, Opmane B, Mutulis F, Mutule I, Petrovska R, Klusa V, et al. The MC4 receptor mediates α-MSH induced release of nucleus accumbens dopamine. NeuroReport. 2001;12:2155–8.")] and consequently food intake and the reinforcing value of food [[96](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR96 "Epstein LH, Temple JL, Neaderhiser BJ, Salis RJ, Erbe RW, Leddy JJ. Food reinforcement, the dopamine D 2 receptor genotype, and energy intake in obese and Nonobese humans. Behav Neurosci. 2007;121:877–86.")]. Additionally, some preclinical studies suggest that melanocortin signaling regulates food reward [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR38 "Kishi T, Aschkenasi CJ, Lee CE, Mountjoy KG, Saper CB, Elmquist JK. Expression of melanocortin 4 receptor mRNA in the central nervous system of the rat. J Comp Neurol. 2003;457:213–35."), [39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR39 "Davis JF, Choi DL, Shurdak JD, Krause EG, Fitzgerald MF, Lipton JW, et al. Central melanocortins modulate mesocorticolimbic activity and food seeking behavior in the rat. Physiol Behav. 2011;102:491–5.")] and food addiction behaviors [[31](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR31 "Cui H, Lutter M. The expression of MC4Rs in D1R neurons regulates food intake and locomotor sensitization to cocaine. Genes Brain Behav. 2013;12:658–65.")] through their genetic interaction [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR48 "Magno FCCM, Guaraná HC, da Fonseca ACP, Pedrosa AP, Zembrzuski VM, Cabello PH et al. Association of the MC4R rs17782313 polymorphism with plasma ghrelin, leptin, IL6 and TNFα concentrations, food intake and eating behaviors in morbidly obese women. Eat Weight Disorders. 2020.")]. The C allele of rs17782313 may contribute to the satiety responsiveness thus patients may eat in the absence of hunger [[97](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR97 "Ho-Urriola J, Guzmán-Guzmán IP, Smalley SV, González A, Weisstaub G, Domínguez-Vásquez P, et al. Melanocortin-4 receptor polymorphism rs17782313: association with obesity and eating in the absence of hunger in Chilean children. Nutrition. 2014;30:145–9.")]. In this light, having two “non-functioning” MC4R alleles, such as CC allele, had probably compromised satiety response significantly, suggesting that the variant rs17782313 could decrease satiety responsiveness with a greater alteration in homozygous than heterozygous individuals [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR53 "Valette M, Bellisle F, Carette C, Poitou C, Dubern B, Paradis G, et al. Eating behaviour in obese patients with melanocortin-4 receptor mutations: A literature review. Int J Obes. 2013;Int J Obes Lond:1027–35.")]. Thus, in the presence of a hypofunction of the MC4R due to the presence of CC genotype, the result is a decreased POMC stimulation with altered energy homeostasis and reward system regulation via the alteration of the mesolimbic dopaminergic and the opioid systems, and a consequent increase of food intake and altered eating behaviors such as FA. Indeed, patients show a high responsiveness to reward perception when exposed to relevant signals (i.e., highly palatable, and intensely processed foods) and may engage in compulsive behaviors to satisfy these intense desires. While the reward system is generally hyporeactive, it becomes hyperreactive to stimuli associated with addiction thus compelling individuals to eat even when not driven by homeostatic signals (i.e., hunger), solely to experience the hedonic and pleasurable effects of consuming highly palatable foods [[98](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR98 "Schulte EM, Grilo CM, Gearhardt AN. Shared and unique mechanisms underlying binge eating disorder and addictive disorders. Clin Psychol Rev. 2016;44:125–39.")].

We observed a significant influence of the rs17782313 polymorphism on psychopathological variables in the group of patients with FA but not in the group without FA. Our analyses suggest that patients with FA and C allele carrier have higher anxiety and depression than controls. This finding aligns with previous research showing that individuals with CC genotype are more likely to consume unhealthy foods (e.g., processed food, energy dense drinks, high fat food) and to experience significantly depressive symptoms [[99](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR99 "Hajmir MM, Mirzababaei A, Clark CCT, Ghaffarian-Ensaf R, Mirzaei K. The interaction between MC4R gene variant (rs17782313) and dominant dietary patterns on depression in obese and overweight women: a cross sectional study. BMC Endocr Disord 2023;23.")]. Furthermore, suggestive findings demonstrated that the MC system has a pivotal role in stress and negative emotional states response, suggesting that it could be a potential treatment target [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR42 "Chaki S, Okuyama S. Involvement of melanocortin-4 receptor in anxiety and depression. Peptides (NY). 2005;26:1952–64."), [43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR43 "Chaki S, Okubo T. Melanocortin-4 receptor antagonists for the treatment of depression and anxiety disorders. Curr Top Med Chem. 2007;7:1145–51.")]. The distribution of the MC4R in the brain suggests a significant involvement of this receptor in the promotion of negative emotional states [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR42 "Chaki S, Okuyama S. Involvement of melanocortin-4 receptor in anxiety and depression. Peptides (NY). 2005;26:1952–64."), [43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR43 "Chaki S, Okubo T. Melanocortin-4 receptor antagonists for the treatment of depression and anxiety disorders. Curr Top Med Chem. 2007;7:1145–51.")]. The MC4R can mediate stress responses and a possible involvement in mood regulation, due to the interaction of the MC4R with the serotoninergic and dopaminergic pathways, has also been suggested [[100](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR100 "Zhou L, Williams T, Lachey JL, Kishi T, Cowley MA, Heisler LK. Serotonergic pathways converge upon central melanocortin systems to regulate energy balance. Peptides (N.Y.). 2005. pp. 1728–32.")]. The MC4R is prominently present also in the hypothalamus, where it is supposed to regulate the activity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis through arginine vasopressin and corticotropin-releasing factor neurons [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR42 "Chaki S, Okuyama S. Involvement of melanocortin-4 receptor in anxiety and depression. Peptides (NY). 2005;26:1952–64."), [43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR43 "Chaki S, Okubo T. Melanocortin-4 receptor antagonists for the treatment of depression and anxiety disorders. Curr Top Med Chem. 2007;7:1145–51.")]. It has been reported that melanocortin elicits anxiogenic-like effects: stimulation of the MC4R may cause anxiety-like behaviors, while the MC4R antagonists may have anxiolytic potential [[42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR42 "Chaki S, Okuyama S. Involvement of melanocortin-4 receptor in anxiety and depression. Peptides (NY). 2005;26:1952–64.")]. Furthermore, the MC4R signaling may play a role in initiating stress-induced synaptic adaptations in the nucleus accumbens. This brain region is linked to reward processing and characterized by a high expression of dopamine [[101](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR101 "Lim BK, Huang KW, Grueter BA, Rothwell PE, Malenka RC. Anhedonia requires MC4R-mediated synaptic adaptations in nucleus accumbens. Nature. 2012;487:183–9.")].

### Strengths and limitations

Some limitations need to be acknowledged, and results should be interpreted cautiously. First, the cross-sectional design precludes us to infer about causality regarding the genetic contribution of the MC system polymorphisms to FA due to the heterogeneity of genetic variations. Further studies with larger sample size and longitudinal design would provide more robust data to explore causality and generalize findings. Second, self-report questionnaires, although validated tools, may be affected by recall bias, leading to underestimation of eating behaviours or affective symptoms. Indeed, psychiatric comorbid symptoms could have affected psychopathology expression because people with obesity, BED and other comorbid major psychiatric disorders exhibit worse eating psychopathology than those without [[102](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR102 "de Fátima Benato Fusco S, Amancio SCP, Pancieri AP, Alves MVMFF, Spiri WC, Braga EM. Anxiety, sleep quality, and binge eating in overweight or obese adults. Rev Esc Enferm USP. 2020;54:1–8."),[103](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR103 "Duarte-Guerra LS, Kortchmar E, Maraviglia ECS, Costa T da, Lasmar S, Morin CM et al. RMR, Longitudinal patterns of comorbidity between anxiety, depression and binge eating symptoms among patients with obesity: A path analysis. J Affect Disord. 2022;303:255–63."),[104](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR104 "Klatzkin RR, Gaffney S, Cyrus K, Bigus E, Brownley KA. Stress-induced eating in women with binge-eating disorder and obesity. Biol Psychol. 2018;131:96–106.")]. The presence of FA was assessed only using the YFAS 2.0. Although the YFAS 2.0 as a valid tool to evaluate addictive-like eating behaviors [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR3 "Gearhardt AN, Hebebrand J. The concept of food addiction helps inform the Understanding of overeating and obesity: debate consensus. Am J Clin Nutr. 2021;113:274–6.")], present results surely need contextualizing the diagnostic limits. Additionally, findings can be interpreted as applying to individuals with obesity, but it is known that FA also occurs among individuals with a healthy or lower BMI [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR11 "Granero R, Hilker I, Agüera Z, Jiménez-Murcia S, Sauchelli S, Islam MA, et al. Food addiction in a Spanish sample of eating disorders: DSM-5 diagnostic subtype differentiation and validation data. Eur Eat Disord Rev. 2014;22:389–96.")].

Furthermore, the study evaluated the effect only of the MC system and the MC4R polymorphisms, and clarifying whether these gene variations have a direct relationship with eating behaviors such as FA is not possible. Other genes (e.g., MC3R, those involved in dopamine regulation or food reward pathways) might also play a role in FA and further research should explore this area over time.

Even if both sexes were investigated, male participants were underrepresented in our sample potentially hindering the detection of any sex-related effects. While studies provide some findings for sex-specific effects [[83](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR83 "Obregón AM, Oyarce K, Santos JL, Valladares M, Goldfield G. Association of the melanocortin 4 receptor gene rs17782313 polymorphism with rewarding value of food and eating behavior in Chilean children. J Physiol Biochem. 2017;73:29–35."), [105](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR105 "Brodowski J, Szkup M, Jurczak A, Wieder-Huszla S, Brodowska A, Laszczyńska M, et al. Searching for the relationship between the parameters of metabolic syndrome and the rs17782313 (T > C) polymorphism of the MC4R gene in postmenopausal women. Clin Interv Aging. 2017;12:549–55."), [106](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40337-025-01387-8#ref-CR106 "Spielberger CD, Gorsuch RL, Lushene RE. Manual for the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. Palo Alto (CA): Consulting Psychologists Press; 1970.")], more research is required to establish a definitive link between the MC4R rs17782313 and sex-specific FA risk. Also, as the causal factors of genetic variants can manifest differently across diverse populations, our findings shed light only on the Caucasian population, which, to the best of our knowledge, was not investigated regarding the effect of the MC4R variations and FA. Importantly, future studies should include more comprehensive behavioural and metabolic measures to better clarify the specificity of the association between MC system polymorphisms and FA, as well as the intricate interactions among genetic, metabolic, and behavioural factors in the aetiology of FA.

Despite these limitations, this study has some noteworthy strengths. It explored the genetic features associated with FA in patients with obesity reporting an association between the MC system variations and the construct of FA, evaluating psychopathological variables, and employing a control group of patients with obesity but without FA.

## Conclusions

The current findings suggest that, when present, FA may represent a peculiar and more specific phenotype of patients with obesity and/or BED potentially requiring targeted therapies. Results of this study support the notion that obesity is not synonymous either with FA or BED and demand to routinely assess the presence of FA and evaluate more accurately patients with obesity and/or BED. Moreover, the findings of the present work may contribute not only to enhance our understanding of the biological mechanisms underlying the food intake regulation but also shed light on the hedonic and behavioural features of the FA.

In conclusion, while FA is not yet incorporated in the current diagnostic systems (i.e., DSM-5 or ICD-11), and lacks well-validated diagnostic criteria, the biological and genetic suggestive findings of this work may support the existence of FA as a distinct clinical phenomenon.

These results underlie the need to considering FA not only for prevention of its long-term complications but also to mitigating and treating excessive eating motivation, high palatable food intake and consequently the weight gain.

## Summary

Dietary patterns high in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been associated with poor diet quality and health outcomes, and are displacing healthier dietary patterns—meals and dishes prepared with fresh and minimally processed foods—in most parts of the world. In the second paper of this Series, we propose a set of government policies aimed at halting and reversing the rise of UPFs worldwide. To date, policies have mainly focused on reducing consumption of foods high in added fats, sugar, and sodium, many of which are UPFs. However, we propose that these efforts be strengthened and expanded to address a broader set of food system drivers influencing the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. This Series paper addresses four food policy domains that correspond to the key dimensions of food system drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption: UPF products, UPF food environments, UPF manufacturers, fast-food corporations, and supermarket corporations retailers, and food supply chains. For each domain, we explore policy options and focus on large-scale food system measures that target areas in greatest need of change, and their potential impacts. We also examine policies to protect, incentivise, and support dietary patterns based on fresh and minimally processed foods, particularly for lower income households. Which policy actions governments decide to prioritise will depend on each country's level of UPF consumption, along with many other issues unique to each country. We emphasise the importance of advancing this agenda in all countries, irrespective of their development status, to promote healthier diets among populations.

## Introduction

The rapid worldwide increase in the availability, marketing, and consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), along with the extensive research literature on their harmful impacts on various aspects of diet quality and their association with a wide range of diseases, have been described in the first paper of this Series by Monteiro and colleagues.1 Defined within the Nova classification system as formulations of food substances and additives containing little or no whole foods, and designed to displace the other three Nova groups (ie, unprocessed or minimally processed foods, processed culinary ingredients, and processed foods) while maximising industry profits,2 UPFs have introduced a new paradigm in nutritional epidemiology, with substantial implications for food policy.

The second paper in this Series examines the policy actions needed for halting and reversing the increase in UPF production, marketing, and consumption. In some settings, such as schools and school food procurement programmes, completely eliminating UPFs would be ideal; however, in other settings, promoting substantial reductions in the production, marketing, and consumption of products would be adequate and in line with current evidence showing that a reduced share of UPFs in diets is associated with better health outcomes.3 Here, we focus on UPF policies that are government led, national, and mandatory to be effective, as evidence shows that voluntary industry actions are insufficient in scope, implementation, and impact.4, 5, 6

We start by outlining key concepts to clarify the need for policy evolution. To date, food policies have primarily aimed to reduce the intake of nutrients linked to chronic diseases from foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS). These policies have largely aimed to shift consumer behaviour through information campaigns and to promote product reformulation. Although these measures have indirectly targeted many UPFs, they fail to address the broader set of issues—particularly UPFs reformulated to achieve nutrient content below thresholds established by regulations. To more effectively reduce the share of UPFs in diets, dedicated policies that explicitly target UPFs are needed to complement the existing nutrient-based approach. Furthermore, food policies should recognise that the responsibility for the rise in UPF-dominated dietary patterns lies less with consumers and more with food corporations, who should be held accountable for their role.

To achieve these goals, we suggest that present policies need to be expanded in at least two directions. First, broadening the policy focus from HFSS foods to HFSS foods and UPFs. We outline approaches to operationalise the identification of UPFs for different policy purposes based on the Nova definition (panel 1).28 Second, we provide options to both strengthen current food environment policies and develop new policies that address systemic drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption, especially by targeting the large global corporations and retailers that shape food environments and food supply chains, and influence policies. The commercial determinants of ultra-processed diets, including the market and political practices of its leading corporations, and strategies for mobilising a global public health response, are outlined in greater detail in the third paper of this Series, by Baker and colleagues.29

Key messages

*   •
The global rise of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) in human diets is linked to poor diet quality and increased risk of several chronic diseases. We identify four distinct dimensions of food systems that have roles in driving the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, and to which policies can and should be addressed: UPF products, food environments, UPF manufacturers and retailers, and food supply chains.

*   •
The current policy focus on decreasing the consumption of foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS), many of which are also ultra-processed, should broaden to also target UPFs. Some countries have already adopted an intermediate stage of targeting UPFs by adding UPF markers to nutrition profiling models used for regulatory purposes.

*   •
Food environment policies should also broaden from focusing on food reformulation to mandatory regulations that aim to address and restrict the marketing, availability, and affordability of UPFs. These policies include changes to taxes and product labelling: Colombia and Mexico have food and beverage taxes along with front-of-package warning labels (with Colombia's laws all based on the same nutrient profile model); Brazil's national school feeding programme has eliminated most UPFs, with 90% of the food required to be whole or minimally processed by 2026; and Chile has integrated front-of-package warning labels on unhealthy foods with restrictions on their marketing—including a ban on television advertising from 0600 h to 2200 h—and prohibition of their sale or promotion in schools. These policies, along with other impactful changes, should be strengthened, coordinated in a mutually reinforcing way, and extended to more countries.

*   •
A potentially wider range of policies could help to address the broader food system and supply chain drivers of production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, including those focused on corporate UPF manufacturers and retailers, fast food corporations, agricultural production, international trade, and environmental impacts. This broader approach is particularly important for preventing an increase in UPF diets in low-income and middle-income countries.

*   •
Policies are particularly needed to directly restrict the market and political power and activities of transnational UPF corporations (including fast-food companies), given their role as primary drivers of UPF consumption. UPF corporations could potentially be the unit of regulation, including their entire portfolios of products, brands, product sales, and marketing and political activities.

*   •
Complementary policies are needed to support the production, availability, and affordability of fresh and minimally processed foods and their preparation as dishes and prepared meals, and address the socioeconomic and gender inequalities that drive demand for UPFs. Few programmes to date address these issues on a national level.

*   •
The prioritisation of these policies will likely depend on each country's stage in the transition towards diets high in UPFs, and on cultural, political, and socioeconomic contexts. However, global action is urgently needed to promote healthier diets.

We identify four key food policy domains to structure our analysis and recommendations: (1) UPF products; (2) food environments; (3) UPF manufacturers and fast-food and supermarket corporations; and (4) food supply chains (see panel 2). These domains reflect essential components of the food systems that collectively drive the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. For each domain, we review existing policies and propose new policy initiatives (see also the table and panel 3). Evidence indicates that multicomponent interventions—those that operate across individual, environmental, and policy levels—are among the most effective strategies.48 However, this Series paper focuses on food environment and systemic food policy interventions, where both the need and potential for meaningful change are greatest, especially in addressing widening health inequalities.49

We recognise that the rising demand for UPFs, most of which are ready to eat or ready to heat, is shaped by broader socioeconomic shifts, including changing work and living patterns and increasing time and financial pressures on households. This demand is further intensified by the large-scale production and aggressive marketing of UPFs. Policies aimed at reducing UPFs will therefore also need to be complemented by policies that increase the availability and affordability of healthy, unprocessed or minimally processed foods (ie, Nova group 1 foods)—including ready-to-consume or ready-to-heat forms, and other time-saving options (panel 4). These efforts should also address the underlying socioeconomic inequalities that drive demand for UPFs for much of the population, including the unequal gendered burden of cooking, feeding children, and other domestic work.

The expansion of food policies targeting HFSS foods to also include UPFs should consider settings where UPFs dominate and affordable alternatives are scarce. In such cases, applying broad policies to all UPFs could harm populations reliant on them. A gradual and selective policy approach, with tailored strategies, might be more appropriate (panel 5).

This Series paper proposes a set of environmental and food systems policy options to support governments in gradually shifting diets away from UPFs. Although we acknowledge that global evidence should be adapted to align with specific policy priorities and contexts across countries, we emphasise that a core set of actions can already be implemented globally to address the urgent need to improve population diets. In this process, innovative and locally grounded responses could also emerge to help address the underlying drivers of UPF-based diets.

## Summary

Dietary patterns high in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been associated with poor diet quality and health outcomes, and are displacing healthier dietary patterns—meals and dishes prepared with fresh and minimally processed foods—in most parts of the world. In the second paper of this Series, we propose a set of government policies aimed at halting and reversing the rise of UPFs worldwide. To date, policies have mainly focused on reducing consumption of foods high in added fats, sugar, and sodium, many of which are UPFs. However, we propose that these efforts be strengthened and expanded to address a broader set of food system drivers influencing the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. This Series paper addresses four food policy domains that correspond to the key dimensions of food system drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption: UPF products, UPF food environments, UPF manufacturers, fast-food corporations, and supermarket corporations retailers, and food supply chains. For each domain, we explore policy options and focus on large-scale food system measures that target areas in greatest need of change, and their potential impacts. We also examine policies to protect, incentivise, and support dietary patterns based on fresh and minimally processed foods, particularly for lower income households. Which policy actions governments decide to prioritise will depend on each country's level of UPF consumption, along with many other issues unique to each country. We emphasise the importance of advancing this agenda in all countries, irrespective of their development status, to promote healthier diets among populations.

## Introduction

The rapid worldwide increase in the availability, marketing, and consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), along with the extensive research literature on their harmful impacts on various aspects of diet quality and their association with a wide range of diseases, have been described in the first paper of this Series by Monteiro and colleagues.1 Defined within the Nova classification system as formulations of food substances and additives containing little or no whole foods, and designed to displace the other three Nova groups (ie, unprocessed or minimally processed foods, processed culinary ingredients, and processed foods) while maximising industry profits,2 UPFs have introduced a new paradigm in nutritional epidemiology, with substantial implications for food policy.

The second paper in this Series examines the policy actions needed for halting and reversing the increase in UPF production, marketing, and consumption. In some settings, such as schools and school food procurement programmes, completely eliminating UPFs would be ideal; however, in other settings, promoting substantial reductions in the production, marketing, and consumption of products would be adequate and in line with current evidence showing that a reduced share of UPFs in diets is associated with better health outcomes.3 Here, we focus on UPF policies that are government led, national, and mandatory to be effective, as evidence shows that voluntary industry actions are insufficient in scope, implementation, and impact.4, 5, 6

We start by outlining key concepts to clarify the need for policy evolution. To date, food policies have primarily aimed to reduce the intake of nutrients linked to chronic diseases from foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS). These policies have largely aimed to shift consumer behaviour through information campaigns and to promote product reformulation. Although these measures have indirectly targeted many UPFs, they fail to address the broader set of issues—particularly UPFs reformulated to achieve nutrient content below thresholds established by regulations. To more effectively reduce the share of UPFs in diets, dedicated policies that explicitly target UPFs are needed to complement the existing nutrient-based approach. Furthermore, food policies should recognise that the responsibility for the rise in UPF-dominated dietary patterns lies less with consumers and more with food corporations, who should be held accountable for their role.

To achieve these goals, we suggest that present policies need to be expanded in at least two directions. First, broadening the policy focus from HFSS foods to HFSS foods and UPFs. We outline approaches to operationalise the identification of UPFs for different policy purposes based on the Nova definition (panel 1).28 Second, we provide options to both strengthen current food environment policies and develop new policies that address systemic drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption, especially by targeting the large global corporations and retailers that shape food environments and food supply chains, and influence policies. The commercial determinants of ultra-processed diets, including the market and political practices of its leading corporations, and strategies for mobilising a global public health response, are outlined in greater detail in the third paper of this Series, by Baker and colleagues.29

Key messages

*   •
The global rise of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) in human diets is linked to poor diet quality and increased risk of several chronic diseases. We identify four distinct dimensions of food systems that have roles in driving the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, and to which policies can and should be addressed: UPF products, food environments, UPF manufacturers and retailers, and food supply chains.

*   •
The current policy focus on decreasing the consumption of foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS), many of which are also ultra-processed, should broaden to also target UPFs. Some countries have already adopted an intermediate stage of targeting UPFs by adding UPF markers to nutrition profiling models used for regulatory purposes.

*   •
Food environment policies should also broaden from focusing on food reformulation to mandatory regulations that aim to address and restrict the marketing, availability, and affordability of UPFs. These policies include changes to taxes and product labelling: Colombia and Mexico have food and beverage taxes along with front-of-package warning labels (with Colombia's laws all based on the same nutrient profile model); Brazil's national school feeding programme has eliminated most UPFs, with 90% of the food required to be whole or minimally processed by 2026; and Chile has integrated front-of-package warning labels on unhealthy foods with restrictions on their marketing—including a ban on television advertising from 0600 h to 2200 h—and prohibition of their sale or promotion in schools. These policies, along with other impactful changes, should be strengthened, coordinated in a mutually reinforcing way, and extended to more countries.

*   •
A potentially wider range of policies could help to address the broader food system and supply chain drivers of production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, including those focused on corporate UPF manufacturers and retailers, fast food corporations, agricultural production, international trade, and environmental impacts. This broader approach is particularly important for preventing an increase in UPF diets in low-income and middle-income countries.

*   •
Policies are particularly needed to directly restrict the market and political power and activities of transnational UPF corporations (including fast-food companies), given their role as primary drivers of UPF consumption. UPF corporations could potentially be the unit of regulation, including their entire portfolios of products, brands, product sales, and marketing and political activities.

*   •
Complementary policies are needed to support the production, availability, and affordability of fresh and minimally processed foods and their preparation as dishes and prepared meals, and address the socioeconomic and gender inequalities that drive demand for UPFs. Few programmes to date address these issues on a national level.

*   •
The prioritisation of these policies will likely depend on each country's stage in the transition towards diets high in UPFs, and on cultural, political, and socioeconomic contexts. However, global action is urgently needed to promote healthier diets.

We identify four key food policy domains to structure our analysis and recommendations: (1) UPF products; (2) food environments; (3) UPF manufacturers and fast-food and supermarket corporations; and (4) food supply chains (see panel 2). These domains reflect essential components of the food systems that collectively drive the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. For each domain, we review existing policies and propose new policy initiatives (see also the table and panel 3). Evidence indicates that multicomponent interventions—those that operate across individual, environmental, and policy levels—are among the most effective strategies.48 However, this Series paper focuses on food environment and systemic food policy interventions, where both the need and potential for meaningful change are greatest, especially in addressing widening health inequalities.49

We recognise that the rising demand for UPFs, most of which are ready to eat or ready to heat, is shaped by broader socioeconomic shifts, including changing work and living patterns and increasing time and financial pressures on households. This demand is further intensified by the large-scale production and aggressive marketing of UPFs. Policies aimed at reducing UPFs will therefore also need to be complemented by policies that increase the availability and affordability of healthy, unprocessed or minimally processed foods (ie, Nova group 1 foods)—including ready-to-consume or ready-to-heat forms, and other time-saving options (panel 4). These efforts should also address the underlying socioeconomic inequalities that drive demand for UPFs for much of the population, including the unequal gendered burden of cooking, feeding children, and other domestic work.

The expansion of food policies targeting HFSS foods to also include UPFs should consider settings where UPFs dominate and affordable alternatives are scarce. In such cases, applying broad policies to all UPFs could harm populations reliant on them. A gradual and selective policy approach, with tailored strategies, might be more appropriate (panel 5).

This Series paper proposes a set of environmental and food systems policy options to support governments in gradually shifting diets away from UPFs. Although we acknowledge that global evidence should be adapted to align with specific policy priorities and contexts across countries, we emphasise that a core set of actions can already be implemented globally to address the urgent need to improve population diets. In this process, innovative and locally grounded responses could also emerge to help address the underlying drivers of UPF-based diets.

## Summary

Dietary patterns high in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been associated with poor diet quality and health outcomes, and are displacing healthier dietary patterns—meals and dishes prepared with fresh and minimally processed foods—in most parts of the world. In the second paper of this Series, we propose a set of government policies aimed at halting and reversing the rise of UPFs worldwide. To date, policies have mainly focused on reducing consumption of foods high in added fats, sugar, and sodium, many of which are UPFs. However, we propose that these efforts be strengthened and expanded to address a broader set of food system drivers influencing the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. This Series paper addresses four food policy domains that correspond to the key dimensions of food system drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption: UPF products, UPF food environments, UPF manufacturers, fast-food corporations, and supermarket corporations retailers, and food supply chains. For each domain, we explore policy options and focus on large-scale food system measures that target areas in greatest need of change, and their potential impacts. We also examine policies to protect, incentivise, and support dietary patterns based on fresh and minimally processed foods, particularly for lower income households. Which policy actions governments decide to prioritise will depend on each country's level of UPF consumption, along with many other issues unique to each country. We emphasise the importance of advancing this agenda in all countries, irrespective of their development status, to promote healthier diets among populations.

## Introduction

The rapid worldwide increase in the availability, marketing, and consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), along with the extensive research literature on their harmful impacts on various aspects of diet quality and their association with a wide range of diseases, have been described in the first paper of this Series by Monteiro and colleagues.1 Defined within the Nova classification system as formulations of food substances and additives containing little or no whole foods, and designed to displace the other three Nova groups (ie, unprocessed or minimally processed foods, processed culinary ingredients, and processed foods) while maximising industry profits,2 UPFs have introduced a new paradigm in nutritional epidemiology, with substantial implications for food policy.

The second paper in this Series examines the policy actions needed for halting and reversing the increase in UPF production, marketing, and consumption. In some settings, such as schools and school food procurement programmes, completely eliminating UPFs would be ideal; however, in other settings, promoting substantial reductions in the production, marketing, and consumption of products would be adequate and in line with current evidence showing that a reduced share of UPFs in diets is associated with better health outcomes.3 Here, we focus on UPF policies that are government led, national, and mandatory to be effective, as evidence shows that voluntary industry actions are insufficient in scope, implementation, and impact.4, 5, 6

We start by outlining key concepts to clarify the need for policy evolution. To date, food policies have primarily aimed to reduce the intake of nutrients linked to chronic diseases from foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS). These policies have largely aimed to shift consumer behaviour through information campaigns and to promote product reformulation. Although these measures have indirectly targeted many UPFs, they fail to address the broader set of issues—particularly UPFs reformulated to achieve nutrient content below thresholds established by regulations. To more effectively reduce the share of UPFs in diets, dedicated policies that explicitly target UPFs are needed to complement the existing nutrient-based approach. Furthermore, food policies should recognise that the responsibility for the rise in UPF-dominated dietary patterns lies less with consumers and more with food corporations, who should be held accountable for their role.

To achieve these goals, we suggest that present policies need to be expanded in at least two directions. First, broadening the policy focus from HFSS foods to HFSS foods and UPFs. We outline approaches to operationalise the identification of UPFs for different policy purposes based on the Nova definition (panel 1).28 Second, we provide options to both strengthen current food environment policies and develop new policies that address systemic drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption, especially by targeting the large global corporations and retailers that shape food environments and food supply chains, and influence policies. The commercial determinants of ultra-processed diets, including the market and political practices of its leading corporations, and strategies for mobilising a global public health response, are outlined in greater detail in the third paper of this Series, by Baker and colleagues.29

Key messages

*   •
The global rise of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) in human diets is linked to poor diet quality and increased risk of several chronic diseases. We identify four distinct dimensions of food systems that have roles in driving the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, and to which policies can and should be addressed: UPF products, food environments, UPF manufacturers and retailers, and food supply chains.

*   •
The current policy focus on decreasing the consumption of foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS), many of which are also ultra-processed, should broaden to also target UPFs. Some countries have already adopted an intermediate stage of targeting UPFs by adding UPF markers to nutrition profiling models used for regulatory purposes.

*   •
Food environment policies should also broaden from focusing on food reformulation to mandatory regulations that aim to address and restrict the marketing, availability, and affordability of UPFs. These policies include changes to taxes and product labelling: Colombia and Mexico have food and beverage taxes along with front-of-package warning labels (with Colombia's laws all based on the same nutrient profile model); Brazil's national school feeding programme has eliminated most UPFs, with 90% of the food required to be whole or minimally processed by 2026; and Chile has integrated front-of-package warning labels on unhealthy foods with restrictions on their marketing—including a ban on television advertising from 0600 h to 2200 h—and prohibition of their sale or promotion in schools. These policies, along with other impactful changes, should be strengthened, coordinated in a mutually reinforcing way, and extended to more countries.

*   •
A potentially wider range of policies could help to address the broader food system and supply chain drivers of production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, including those focused on corporate UPF manufacturers and retailers, fast food corporations, agricultural production, international trade, and environmental impacts. This broader approach is particularly important for preventing an increase in UPF diets in low-income and middle-income countries.

*   •
Policies are particularly needed to directly restrict the market and political power and activities of transnational UPF corporations (including fast-food companies), given their role as primary drivers of UPF consumption. UPF corporations could potentially be the unit of regulation, including their entire portfolios of products, brands, product sales, and marketing and political activities.

*   •
Complementary policies are needed to support the production, availability, and affordability of fresh and minimally processed foods and their preparation as dishes and prepared meals, and address the socioeconomic and gender inequalities that drive demand for UPFs. Few programmes to date address these issues on a national level.

*   •
The prioritisation of these policies will likely depend on each country's stage in the transition towards diets high in UPFs, and on cultural, political, and socioeconomic contexts. However, global action is urgently needed to promote healthier diets.

We identify four key food policy domains to structure our analysis and recommendations: (1) UPF products; (2) food environments; (3) UPF manufacturers and fast-food and supermarket corporations; and (4) food supply chains (see panel 2). These domains reflect essential components of the food systems that collectively drive the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. For each domain, we review existing policies and propose new policy initiatives (see also the table and panel 3). Evidence indicates that multicomponent interventions—those that operate across individual, environmental, and policy levels—are among the most effective strategies.48 However, this Series paper focuses on food environment and systemic food policy interventions, where both the need and potential for meaningful change are greatest, especially in addressing widening health inequalities.49

We recognise that the rising demand for UPFs, most of which are ready to eat or ready to heat, is shaped by broader socioeconomic shifts, including changing work and living patterns and increasing time and financial pressures on households. This demand is further intensified by the large-scale production and aggressive marketing of UPFs. Policies aimed at reducing UPFs will therefore also need to be complemented by policies that increase the availability and affordability of healthy, unprocessed or minimally processed foods (ie, Nova group 1 foods)—including ready-to-consume or ready-to-heat forms, and other time-saving options (panel 4). These efforts should also address the underlying socioeconomic inequalities that drive demand for UPFs for much of the population, including the unequal gendered burden of cooking, feeding children, and other domestic work.

The expansion of food policies targeting HFSS foods to also include UPFs should consider settings where UPFs dominate and affordable alternatives are scarce. In such cases, applying broad policies to all UPFs could harm populations reliant on them. A gradual and selective policy approach, with tailored strategies, might be more appropriate (panel 5).

This Series paper proposes a set of environmental and food systems policy options to support governments in gradually shifting diets away from UPFs. Although we acknowledge that global evidence should be adapted to align with specific policy priorities and contexts across countries, we emphasise that a core set of actions can already be implemented globally to address the urgent need to improve population diets. In this process, innovative and locally grounded responses could also emerge to help address the underlying drivers of UPF-based diets.

## Summary

Dietary patterns high in ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been associated with poor diet quality and health outcomes, and are displacing healthier dietary patterns—meals and dishes prepared with fresh and minimally processed foods—in most parts of the world. In the second paper of this Series, we propose a set of government policies aimed at halting and reversing the rise of UPFs worldwide. To date, policies have mainly focused on reducing consumption of foods high in added fats, sugar, and sodium, many of which are UPFs. However, we propose that these efforts be strengthened and expanded to address a broader set of food system drivers influencing the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. This Series paper addresses four food policy domains that correspond to the key dimensions of food system drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption: UPF products, UPF food environments, UPF manufacturers, fast-food corporations, and supermarket corporations retailers, and food supply chains. For each domain, we explore policy options and focus on large-scale food system measures that target areas in greatest need of change, and their potential impacts. We also examine policies to protect, incentivise, and support dietary patterns based on fresh and minimally processed foods, particularly for lower income households. Which policy actions governments decide to prioritise will depend on each country's level of UPF consumption, along with many other issues unique to each country. We emphasise the importance of advancing this agenda in all countries, irrespective of their development status, to promote healthier diets among populations.

## Introduction

The rapid worldwide increase in the availability, marketing, and consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), along with the extensive research literature on their harmful impacts on various aspects of diet quality and their association with a wide range of diseases, have been described in the first paper of this Series by Monteiro and colleagues.1 Defined within the Nova classification system as formulations of food substances and additives containing little or no whole foods, and designed to displace the other three Nova groups (ie, unprocessed or minimally processed foods, processed culinary ingredients, and processed foods) while maximising industry profits,2 UPFs have introduced a new paradigm in nutritional epidemiology, with substantial implications for food policy.

The second paper in this Series examines the policy actions needed for halting and reversing the increase in UPF production, marketing, and consumption. In some settings, such as schools and school food procurement programmes, completely eliminating UPFs would be ideal; however, in other settings, promoting substantial reductions in the production, marketing, and consumption of products would be adequate and in line with current evidence showing that a reduced share of UPFs in diets is associated with better health outcomes.3 Here, we focus on UPF policies that are government led, national, and mandatory to be effective, as evidence shows that voluntary industry actions are insufficient in scope, implementation, and impact.4, 5, 6

We start by outlining key concepts to clarify the need for policy evolution. To date, food policies have primarily aimed to reduce the intake of nutrients linked to chronic diseases from foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS). These policies have largely aimed to shift consumer behaviour through information campaigns and to promote product reformulation. Although these measures have indirectly targeted many UPFs, they fail to address the broader set of issues—particularly UPFs reformulated to achieve nutrient content below thresholds established by regulations. To more effectively reduce the share of UPFs in diets, dedicated policies that explicitly target UPFs are needed to complement the existing nutrient-based approach. Furthermore, food policies should recognise that the responsibility for the rise in UPF-dominated dietary patterns lies less with consumers and more with food corporations, who should be held accountable for their role.

To achieve these goals, we suggest that present policies need to be expanded in at least two directions. First, broadening the policy focus from HFSS foods to HFSS foods and UPFs. We outline approaches to operationalise the identification of UPFs for different policy purposes based on the Nova definition (panel 1).28 Second, we provide options to both strengthen current food environment policies and develop new policies that address systemic drivers of UPF production, marketing, and consumption, especially by targeting the large global corporations and retailers that shape food environments and food supply chains, and influence policies. The commercial determinants of ultra-processed diets, including the market and political practices of its leading corporations, and strategies for mobilising a global public health response, are outlined in greater detail in the third paper of this Series, by Baker and colleagues.29

Key messages

*   •
The global rise of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) in human diets is linked to poor diet quality and increased risk of several chronic diseases. We identify four distinct dimensions of food systems that have roles in driving the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, and to which policies can and should be addressed: UPF products, food environments, UPF manufacturers and retailers, and food supply chains.

*   •
The current policy focus on decreasing the consumption of foods high in fats, sugars, and salt (HFSS), many of which are also ultra-processed, should broaden to also target UPFs. Some countries have already adopted an intermediate stage of targeting UPFs by adding UPF markers to nutrition profiling models used for regulatory purposes.

*   •
Food environment policies should also broaden from focusing on food reformulation to mandatory regulations that aim to address and restrict the marketing, availability, and affordability of UPFs. These policies include changes to taxes and product labelling: Colombia and Mexico have food and beverage taxes along with front-of-package warning labels (with Colombia's laws all based on the same nutrient profile model); Brazil's national school feeding programme has eliminated most UPFs, with 90% of the food required to be whole or minimally processed by 2026; and Chile has integrated front-of-package warning labels on unhealthy foods with restrictions on their marketing—including a ban on television advertising from 0600 h to 2200 h—and prohibition of their sale or promotion in schools. These policies, along with other impactful changes, should be strengthened, coordinated in a mutually reinforcing way, and extended to more countries.

*   •
A potentially wider range of policies could help to address the broader food system and supply chain drivers of production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs, including those focused on corporate UPF manufacturers and retailers, fast food corporations, agricultural production, international trade, and environmental impacts. This broader approach is particularly important for preventing an increase in UPF diets in low-income and middle-income countries.

*   •
Policies are particularly needed to directly restrict the market and political power and activities of transnational UPF corporations (including fast-food companies), given their role as primary drivers of UPF consumption. UPF corporations could potentially be the unit of regulation, including their entire portfolios of products, brands, product sales, and marketing and political activities.

*   •
Complementary policies are needed to support the production, availability, and affordability of fresh and minimally processed foods and their preparation as dishes and prepared meals, and address the socioeconomic and gender inequalities that drive demand for UPFs. Few programmes to date address these issues on a national level.

*   •
The prioritisation of these policies will likely depend on each country's stage in the transition towards diets high in UPFs, and on cultural, political, and socioeconomic contexts. However, global action is urgently needed to promote healthier diets.

We identify four key food policy domains to structure our analysis and recommendations: (1) UPF products; (2) food environments; (3) UPF manufacturers and fast-food and supermarket corporations; and (4) food supply chains (see panel 2). These domains reflect essential components of the food systems that collectively drive the production, marketing, and consumption of UPFs. For each domain, we review existing policies and propose new policy initiatives (see also the table and panel 3). Evidence indicates that multicomponent interventions—those that operate across individual, environmental, and policy levels—are among the most effective strategies.48 However, this Series paper focuses on food environment and systemic food policy interventions, where both the need and potential for meaningful change are greatest, especially in addressing widening health inequalities.49

We recognise that the rising demand for UPFs, most of which are ready to eat or ready to heat, is shaped by broader socioeconomic shifts, including changing work and living patterns and increasing time and financial pressures on households. This demand is further intensified by the large-scale production and aggressive marketing of UPFs. Policies aimed at reducing UPFs will therefore also need to be complemented by policies that increase the availability and affordability of healthy, unprocessed or minimally processed foods (ie, Nova group 1 foods)—including ready-to-consume or ready-to-heat forms, and other time-saving options (panel 4). These efforts should also address the underlying socioeconomic inequalities that drive demand for UPFs for much of the population, including the unequal gendered burden of cooking, feeding children, and other domestic work.

The expansion of food policies targeting HFSS foods to also include UPFs should consider settings where UPFs dominate and affordable alternatives are scarce. In such cases, applying broad policies to all UPFs could harm populations reliant on them. A gradual and selective policy approach, with tailored strategies, might be more appropriate (panel 5).

This Series paper proposes a set of environmental and food systems policy options to support governments in gradually shifting diets away from UPFs. Although we acknowledge that global evidence should be adapted to align with specific policy priorities and contexts across countries, we emphasise that a core set of actions can already be implemented globally to address the urgent need to improve population diets. In this process, innovative and locally grounded responses could also emerge to help address the underlying drivers of UPF-based diets.

## Discussion

The mechanism linking UPF intake to a higher risk of all-cause mortality remains inconclusive. However, several potential factors may explain this positive association. Firstly, high UPF consumption typically involves higher fat, salt, and carbohydrate intake, all of which have been shown to increase the risk of cardiovascular events and other chronic non-communicable diseases by promoting inflammation levels, oxidative stress, thrombosis, or other pathological processes [[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR4)]. Secondly, food additives including emulsifiers, sweeteners, colorants, and micro- and nanoparticles, are commonly added to UPFs, which have been shown to affect the gut microbiome, leading to reduced diversity and shifts in bacterial populations, such as more harmful _Shigella_ and fewer beneficial _Lachnospira_ and _Roseburia_ [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR34)]. This may impair gut function, contribute to metabolic diseases, and thus lead to other adverse outcomes. Thirdly, individuals who consume unhealthy diets are also likely to engage in unhealthy lifestyles, including excessive smoking and alcohol consumption, as well as a lack of physical activity. All of which are high-risk factors for cardiovascular events and mortality [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR35), [36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR36), [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR37), [38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR38)]. Lastly, the health effects of UPFs could be linked to their organoleptic properties, which may lead to an increased eating speed and a delay in satiety signals, resulting in higher overall food intake and poor health outcomes [[39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR39)].

The findings of this research suggest a potential need for dietary guidelines and policies aimed at reducing UPF consumption, although further investigation is required to establish robust causal links. Promoting healthy dietary patterns remains a critical public health goal for maintaining overall population health and extending lifespan. Preliminary insights from policy experiments in early-adopter regions indicate that strategies such as front-of-pack labeling, taxation, and marketing restrictions could reduce UPF consumption by up to 30% [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR40)]. However, comprehensive research is needed to further refine these policies and evaluate their broader health impacts. Furthermore, these strategies should be carefully considered, particularly for regions with lower socioeconomic status, who may rely on UPFs owing to affordability and convenience. Implementing subsidies for healthier foods and improving access to fresh produce could help ensure equitable policy outcomes [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13643-025-02800-8#ref-CR41)].

Summary: 
The systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 prospective cohort studies (1,148,387 participants) provides strong evidence that higher consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality. Compared to the lowest intake, the highest UPF intake conferred a 15% higher risk (HR=1.15, 95% CI 1.09–1.22), and each 10% increment in UPF intake was associated with a 10% higher risk (HR=1.10, 95% CI 1.04–1.16), with a significant linear dose-response relationship. The authors discuss potential mechanisms including inflammation, oxidative stress, gut microbiome disruption (e.g., reduced diversity, harmful bacterial shifts), unhealthy lifestyle clustering, and altered satiety signaling. Policy approaches mentioned include dietary guidelines, front-of-pack labeling, taxation, and marketing restrictions, which could reduce UPF consumption by up to 30%, alongside subsidies for healthier foods to address equity. Notably, the content does not address addictive properties or brain mechanisms of UPFs, which are outside the scope of this mortality-focused meta-analysis.
